## Background

The GST is a 5% value-added tax on most of what households buy. In the
five provinces with an HST, it is combined with a provincial sales tax
into one tax at a higher rate. This assignment looks only at the federal
5%, which is charged on the same goods and services in every province.

Not everything is taxed. Some goods and services are **zero-rated**: no
GST is charged when they are sold, and the seller can claim back the GST
it paid on its own inputs. Basic groceries, prescription drugs and
medical devices are zero-rated. Others are **exempt**: no GST is charged
when they are sold, but the seller cannot claim back the GST it paid on
its inputs. Residential rent, most health and dental services, child
care, education, insurance and financial services are exempt.

Consumption taxes are often called regressive. Lower-income households
spend a larger share of what they earn, so a tax on spending takes a
larger share of their income. In class we saw three reasons to be
careful with that claim:

-   a household's income in one year can be a poor guide to how well
    off it is over its lifetime;
-   zero-rating and exemptions take the GST off some of what
    lower-income households spend the most on;
-   the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit (called the GST/HST
    credit until July 2026) gives lower-income families a payment that
    does not depend on what they buy.

In this assignment you will use the spending records of over 5,000
Canadian households to work out how much GST households pay at each
level of income, measured against their income and against their
spending. You will then simulate the benefit, and ask what would happen
if the government taxed food and gave the money back through the
benefit instead. Throughout, assume that buyers bear the whole tax, so
that prices are higher by the full amount of the GST. This is the usual
assumption in calculations like these, and it is the one we questioned
in class when we covered tax incidence.

## The data

The data come from Statistics Canada's Survey of Household Spending
(SHS) for 2023. Each row is one household. The file is an extract from
the survey's public use microdata file: it keeps 59 of its 398
variables, with Statistics Canada's own variable names and codes. One
variable has been changed to keep things simple: in this file, `FD003`
(food bought in stores) leaves out candy and snack foods, which are in
`FD821` and `FD883`. The
spending variables are what the household spent in the year, in
dollars, including sales taxes.

Read these notes before you start. They are adapted from Statistics
Canada's user guide for the file.

-   **No weights.** The survey sampled some kinds of households more
    heavily than others, older households in particular, and Statistics
    Canada provides weights to correct for that. To keep things simple,
    this file leaves the weights out, and you will treat every household
    the same. Your results will show the same patterns as Statistics
    Canada's published figures, but some numbers will differ, and older
    households will make up more of the file than they do of the
    population.
-   **Provinces only.** Statistics Canada's estimates for Canada cover
    the ten provinces. The file also has households from the three
    territorial capitals (`PROV` = 63), which you will drop.
-   **Diary spending.** Some spending, such as gasoline, was recorded in
    a one-week diary and multiplied by 52 to make it annual. One
    household's figure for such an item can be far off: a household that
    happened not to buy gas that week shows \$0 for the year. Averages
    over many households are accurate.
-   **Confidentiality.** To protect the households in the survey,
    Statistics Canada has capped some very large values and slightly
    altered others. A handful of households report income taxes larger
    than their income.

**Household variables**

| Variable | Description |
|:-------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| `CASEID` | Household identifier |
| `PROV` | Province: 10 Newfoundland and Labrador, 11 Prince Edward Island, 12 Nova Scotia, 13 New Brunswick, 24 Quebec, 35 Ontario, 46 Manitoba, 47 Saskatchewan, 48 Alberta, 59 British Columbia, 63 territorial capitals |
| `HHTYPE6` | Household type: 1 one person, 2 couple without children, 3 couple with children, 4 couple with other related or unrelated people, 5 lone-parent family, 6 other household |
| `HHSIZE` | Number of people in the household (4 means 4 or more) |
| `RP_AGEGP` | Age of the household's reference person: 1 under 30, 2 30 to 39, 3 40 to 54, 4 55 to 64, 5 65 to 74, 6 75 and over |
| `HHTOTINC` | Total household income before tax, from all sources, including government transfers |
| `TX010` | Income taxes paid by the household |
| `TC001` | Total current consumption: the sum of all the spending variables below |

## Question 2: The GST in Each Quintile

**(a)** Use the **Treat as** column in the table of spending variables
above to calculate each household's GST. For the four variables marked **You
decide**, decide whether most of the spending is taxed or untaxed. You
will explain your choices in your comment. Then create, for each
household in `hh`:

-   `untaxed`: spending on everything that is zero-rated, exempt or
    otherwise untaxed;
-   `taxable`: total consumption, `TC001`, minus `untaxed`;
-   `gst`: the GST included in taxable spending. The GST is 5% of
    pre-tax spending, so

    $$
    \text{post-tax spending} = 1.05 \times \text{pre-tax spending}
    $$

    The amounts in the data are what households paid, so `taxable` is
    post-tax spending. Pre-tax spending is therefore `taxable` / 1.05,
    and the GST is 5% of that:

    $$
    \text{gst} = 0.05 \times \frac{\text{taxable}}{1.05}
    $$

    For example, \$105 of taxed spending is \$100 of pre-tax spending
    plus \$5 of GST.

*Hints.*

-   There are fewer untaxed variables than taxed ones, so it is quicker
    to add up the untaxed ones and subtract their sum from `TC001`.
-   To check your work, `summary(hh$taxable)` should show no negative
    values.

## Question 3: The Benefit and Zero-Rated Food

The Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit for July 2026 to
June 2027 pays up to \$679 a year to a single person and \$890 to a
couple, plus \$234 for each child. It is reduced by 5% of family net
income above \$46,432. Simulate it for each household in `hh`, using
these simplified rules:

-   count one adult in one-person households and lone-parent families
    (`HHTYPE6` 1 or 5), and two adults in every other household;
-   the maximum benefit is \$679 with one adult or \$890 with two, plus
    \$234 for each other person in the household (`HHSIZE` minus the
    number of adults);
-   `benefit` is the maximum benefit minus 5% of the part of `HHTOTINC`
    above \$46,432, but it cannot be less than 0.

Also create `food_gst`, the GST households would pay if the zero-rated
food they buy in stores were taxed at 5%. Assume they would buy the same
food at the same prices before tax. Food is not taxed now, so the
amounts are already prices before tax, and `food_gst` is 0.05 times
`FD003`.

Then, for each quintile, calculate the averages of `benefit`,
`food_gst`, `gst` and `atinc`, and store the result in a data frame
called `q3`. Add two variables to it:

-   `gst_income`: average GST as a percentage of average after-tax
    income, as in Question 2;
-   `net_income`: average GST minus average benefit, as a percentage of
    average after-tax income.
